title: "A" Camshaft Position Actuator Circuit (Bank 2)
plain: The engine uses an electric oil control valve to adjust the "A" (usually intake) camshaft timing on bank 2. The computer found a problem in the wiring or the valve itself, such as an open or shorted circuit.
symptoms: Engine may run fine but with a light on

causes.name: Failed camshaft oil control valve (VVT solenoid)
Damaged wiring or loose connector at the solenoid
Oil leaking into the solenoid connector
Engine computer driver fault

checks: Inspect the solenoid connector for oil, corrosion or a loose fit
Measure the solenoid resistance and compare to spec
Command the solenoid on with a scan tool and watch for a response
fix: Usually a new camshaft oil control valve, or a wiring or connector repair.

cost.job: Replace camshaft oil control valve (VVT solenoid)

title: "A" Camshaft Position - Timing Over-Advanced or System Performance (Bank 2)
plain: The "A" (usually intake) camshaft on bank 2 is further ahead of, or not following, the position the computer asked for. The variable valve timing system is not controlling it correctly.
symptoms: Possible stalling or rattle at startup

causes.name: Low, dirty or wrong-grade engine oil
Sticking or failed camshaft oil control valve
Camshaft phaser stuck or worn
Stretched timing chain or jumped timing
Clogged oil screen at the oil control valve

checks: Check the oil level and change it if dirty or overdue, using the correct grade
Remove and inspect the oil control valve for sludge or a stuck spool
Check cam timing values with a scan tool before replacing the phaser or chain
fix: Start with an oil change. If it comes back, the oil control valve is the most common fix, then the phaser or timing chain.

cost.job: Replace camshaft oil control valve (VVT solenoid)

examples: Often paired with P0012 on the Ford 5.4L 3-valve V8 when the cam phasers wear

title: Intake Valve Control Solenoid Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1)
plain: The intake valve control solenoid on bank 1 helps change valve timing or lift. The computer sees that the solenoid circuit is working, but the result is not what it expected.

causes.name: Sticking valve control solenoid
Low, dirty or wrong-grade engine oil
Wiring or connector problem at the solenoid
Worn camshaft phaser or timing components

checks: Check the oil level and condition
Inspect the solenoid and its screen for sludge
Check the solenoid wiring and resistance
fix: Often an oil change, then a new valve control solenoid if the code returns.

title: "B" Camshaft Profile Control Circuit/Open (Bank 1)
plain: Some engines can switch between two camshaft lobe shapes, one for economy and one for power. The computer found an open or broken connection in the control circuit for the "B" camshaft switching on bank 1.
symptoms: Less power at higher engine speeds
Engine may stay in one cam mode

causes.name: Damaged wiring or loose connector to the cam profile solenoid
Failed cam profile switching solenoid
Low or dirty engine oil affecting the switching mechanism
Engine computer driver fault

checks: Check the oil level and condition
Inspect the solenoid connector and wiring
Test the solenoid resistance and command it with a scan tool
fix: Usually a wiring repair or a new cam profile switching solenoid.

title: HO2S Heater Control Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 1)
plain: Oxygen sensors have a built-in heater so they start working soon after a cold start. The computer found a fault, such as an open circuit, in the heater circuit of the upstream (before the catalytic converter) oxygen sensor on bank 1.
symptoms: Usually no change in how the car drives
Fuel economy may drop slightly, mostly after cold starts

causes.name: Failed heater inside the oxygen sensor
Blown fuse for the oxygen sensor heaters
Damaged or melted wiring near the exhaust
Corroded or loose sensor connector
Engine computer heater driver fault

checks: Check the oxygen sensor heater fuse
Inspect the sensor wiring for melted or rubbed-through spots near the exhaust
Measure the heater resistance at the sensor and compare to spec
fix: Most often a new oxygen sensor. If the fuse is blown, find the short that blew it before replacing the sensor.

title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve Control Circuit
plain: On turbocharged or supercharged engines, a bypass (blow-off or diverter) valve releases boost pressure when you lift off the gas. The computer found a fault, such as an open circuit, in the circuit that controls this valve.
symptoms: Loss of power or slow boost build-up
Possible limp mode or whooshing noise

causes.name: Failed bypass (diverter) valve solenoid
Damaged wiring or loose connector
Cracked vacuum hose to the valve, on vacuum-operated types
Engine computer driver fault

checks: Inspect the valve connector and wiring
Check vacuum hoses around the turbo for cracks
Command the valve with a scan tool and listen or watch for it to move
fix: Usually a new bypass valve or a wiring repair.

title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve Control Circuit Range/Performance
plain: The bypass (blow-off or diverter) valve on a boosted engine is not responding the way the computer expects, even though the circuit is not fully open or shorted.
symptoms: Loss of power or uneven boost

causes.name: Sticking or worn bypass valve
Torn diaphragm in the bypass valve
Boost or vacuum leak near the valve
Intermittent wiring fault

checks: Inspect the bypass valve and hoses for leaks or tears
Check the wiring and connector
Watch commanded vs actual boost on a scan tool
fix: Usually a new bypass valve, or repair of a leaking boost hose.

title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Boost Control "A" Position Exceeded Learning Limit
plain: The computer learns the normal resting and travel positions of the boost control actuator (often the wastegate or variable vane control). The "A" actuator position has drifted beyond what the computer will accept.
symptoms: Too little or too much boost

causes.name: Worn or sticking wastegate or vane mechanism
Faulty boost control actuator or its position sensor
Actuator not set up or relearned after a repair
Carbon buildup in the turbo

checks: Check whether the turbo or actuator was recently replaced and needs a relearn
Inspect the actuator linkage for binding
Run the actuator test or relearn with a scan tool
fix: Often an actuator relearn or a new boost actuator; a sticking turbo may need cleaning or replacement.

title: "A" Camshaft Profile Control Performance/Stuck Off (Bank 1)
plain: Some engines can switch between two camshaft lobe shapes. On bank 1, the computer found the "A" cam switching system not switching properly or stuck in its off position.
symptoms: Less power at higher engine speeds

causes.name: Low, dirty or wrong-grade engine oil
Sticking cam profile switching solenoid
Low oil pressure to the switching mechanism
Worn or sticking cam follower or locking pin

checks: Check the oil level and condition
Check oil pressure
Inspect the switching solenoid and its screen for sludge
fix: Often an oil change and a new switching solenoid. Mechanical wear inside the valvetrain is less common.
